#4808. Tesla’s rocket-shaped Robotaxi map in Houston is partly ‘fake’

Tesla’s new rocket-shaped Robotaxi service area in Houston includes parts of downtown where the service won’t actually pick you up, according to Ethan McKanna, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker and former Tesla employee.

McKanna rode the service after Monday’s expansion and called Houston “by far the most egregious ‘fake’ AV service area” he has seen. One trip quote had him spending about 40 minutes in a Robotaxi to go two blocks.

On Monday, Tesla expanded its Houston Robotaxi geofence into the shape of a rocket. It took the small launch zone in northwest Harris County and stretched it into a long corridor down to downtown and Bellaire, announced with “Houston, we have liftoff.”

McKanna runs Robotaxi Tracker, the crowdsourced site that tracks Tesla’s Robotaxi fleet and service areas, and he worked at Tesla this summer, so he knows the program better than most. He went to Houston to try it out. Here’s what he posted last night:

Another thing. Often AV service area maps advertised are kind of fake- they don’t actually go to everywhere in the polygon the provider publishes. Robotaxi Houston is probably by far the most egregious ‘fake’ AV service area I’ve seenI get they were doing it so they could get… https://t.co/ILXIkmwGVp pic.twitter.com/yUfswZhQKF

The video shows the Robotaxi app with a pickup pin dropped in downtown Houston, well inside the polygon Tesla published. The app refuses it: “Location not available. Move the map to select a different location.”

McKanna acknowledged that AV service area maps are often “kind of fake,” since operators don’t serve every street inside the polygon they advertise. But he singled out Houston as the worst case he’s seen and said he understands Tesla did it “so they could get the starship shape,” which doesn’t seem like a good reason to fake availability.

The day before, he posted a trip quote that shows what this looks like for a rider:

40 min ride to cross 2 blocks downtown.this is pretty rough pic.twitter.com/n8kP4s9evT

The app quoted a 2:05 pm pickup on the east side of downtown and a 2:48 pm drop-off at Houston Police Department headquarters on Travis Street, a couple of blocks away. Instead of cutting across downtown, the planned route runs south through Midtown and the Museum District to the Texas Medical Center area, then loops back north.

McKanna’s read is that the Robotaxi appears to be avoiding railroad crossings downtown, and he said it fits with “other strange routing in Houston.” He expects Tesla to fix it.

To be fair, he wasn’t down on the service overall. He wrote that, apart from that issue, it “feels really good in Houston,” with reasonable wait times and “significantly better driving than my recent Waymo rides.”

Tesla isn’t the only one. On Tuesday, Robotaxi Tracker reported that Waymo’s Orlando service area had shrunk by 10 square miles, down 8.4% to 109 square miles. McKanna explained what happened:

Orlando’s airport was inside the map Waymo published, but McKanna checked the app and it won’t let riders set the airport as a drop-off yet. So the tracker took it out. Waymo’s airport service might be rolling out soon, and someone got ahead of the announcement.

That’s an airport on the edge of the map. In Houston, the dead zone is in the middle of downtown.

The key to understanding Tesla is the stockholders are the real customers, Elon looks at actual paying customers of his products as patsies or marks who will willingly serve as unpaid beta (or alpha) testers and who will be the ones paying or going to jail when something goes wrong.

First, a big thanks to Ethan. Tesla shares very little data about its Robotaxi program, and Robotaxi Tracker has become the best independent source on where Tesla’s fleet actually operates and how big it is. And as Orlando shows, he holds Waymo to the same standard.

Every AV operator has gaps in its map, Waymo included. But Waymo’s Orlando gap is an airport on the edge of the map that it’s likely about to add. Tesla’s Houston gap is downtown, and it drew a rocket first and figured out where the cars could actually go second.

Service and product should always outrank marketing, and that’s clearly not the case with Tesla’s Robotaxi. People rely on those maps to know if Tesla offers the service where they are. Faking the map just to make a rocket shape is completely stupid. Do better.

#4807. We Need to Talk About Women and Social Anxiety

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 7, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Consciousness-raising has its origins in the second-wave feminism of the 1960s, notably with the New York Radical Women, perhaps best known for staging a protest at the 1968 Miss America pageant. Feminist consciousness-raising aimed to help women realise that a lot of their problems were not individual, but instead resulted from institutional sexism—being caged by traditional gender roles is one example. A popular slogan of the time, "the personal is political," encapsulates the same sentiment, for it puts forth that oppression within domestic spheres (the home, family, and relationships) is not separate from wider power structures in society (gender inequality).

In 2026, we’re arguably in the age of post-feminism, where conventional wisdom often holds that the work of the women’s movement has been done.

While we’ve certainly come a long way, what came to the fore when I interviewed socially anxious women as part of my research (Masters, 2024) was that we still have some way to go. That is to say, a lot of these women’s experiences not only evoked sexism, but they described such experiences as being a key part of their social anxiety.

Ellen* described regularly enduring street harassment, and how this was central to her social anxiety: "[I]t constantly happens […] it’s an everyday battle, so therefore why would you not internalise […] take that with you and worry about it the next day?"

Ria* told me about making suggestions for improvements in work meetings, only for them to get ignored—except these same things were later implemented when male colleagues brought them up. She spoke about the effect this had on her self-confidence, adding, "[W]hen it happens more than once […] eventually, it’s going to chip away at you, isn’t it?"

These experiences are "everyday," but they’re underpinned by bigger issues: Think about Ria’s being undermined in the workplace and the gender pay gap—6.8 percent in 2026 (Office for National Statistics, 2026)—or Ellen’s street harassment and sexual violence—1 in 4 women over the age of 16 in England and Wales has been raped or sexually assaulted (ONS, 2025). (For examples of even more overt and, frankly, frightening misogynistic experiences, see Laura Bates’s Everyday Sexism Project.)

Ellen’s and Ria’s experiences could be characterised as more subtle nods to sexism, sometimes so subtle that those to whom they happen might question whether they’re being too sensitive. Another woman I interviewed, Farah, told me that when she would openly decry occurrences such as these, people would often respond to her by saying "Well, you’re so sensitive."

This only stokes social anxiety further: In particular, it promotes what psychologist Gillian Butler dubs the "post-mortem" of events (2016). We might think, "Did I get offended too easily? Was it my fault? What if I deserved it? Was it even as bad as I thought? Was I just imagining it? Why is no one else speaking up?"

Professor of Counselling Psychology Derald Wing Sue calls events like those described above "microaggressions" (2010). Crucially, Sue says that when these happen to us, we search for patterns in terms of similar past experiences. In so doing, we often see a link between these experiences and an aspect of our identity: being a woman, being from an ethnic minority, or being disabled, to name but a few.

The very nature of social anxiety is a fear of being negatively evaluated, and for this fear to exist at all, we need to believe that such negative evaluation is warranted. And it wouldn’t be warranted unless we perceive ourselves to be not good enough, or odd, or bad in some way—not like everybody else. So, as I’ve argued elsewhere (Masters, 2024), it’s possible that socially anxious women attribute these events not to their identities, but to themselves, as individuals.

Given this, it can be very heartening to learn that, actually, some of these experiences are like everybody else’s: They don't just happen to us. I’m not talking about a type of schadenfreude, or taking pleasure in another’s misfortune, but rather, realising that we’re not alone in these experiences, in feeling angry about them, or in feeling more socially anxious in light of them. It’s not us that’s at fault, and the way we feel—frustrated, afraid of being judged, lacking in confidence—is quite understandable.

Perhaps the most straightforward way to have these kinds of revelations is by talking to others. It still does feel a bit taboo, doesn’t it, talking openly about sexism, like you might just be dismissed as "moaning" or told that women have it so good now, or that our perceived injustices are down to our personal choices. But if we don’t talk about it, we’ll never have an appreciation that these things are happening to other women too—and, often, they feel much the same way as we do.

"Talking about it" doesn’t need to be a formal undertaking: You don’t need to set up a monthly consciousness-raising group in your neighbourhood for fellow socially anxious women. But, hey, if you want to, go right ahead—and let me know when and where it is so I can come!

Of course, "talking" on its own isn’t going to change long-entrenched societal structures and injustices overnight, but it’s certainly a start. The New York Radical Women themselves had humble beginnings: At the outset, they were just five in number, and met regularly in members’ apartments across Manhattan. It might be as simple as asking a friend, "Hey, has this ever happened to you?" or "Do you ever feel like…?"

Activist Judi Chamberlin talks about the importance of consciousness-raising not in terms of feminism, but for those experiencing mental distress. She says it "helps people to see that their so-called symptoms are indications of real problems […] Instead of believing that they have a defect in their psychic makeup (or neurochemical system), participants learn to recognize the oppressive conditions in their daily lives."

Consciousness-raising can thus provide the means with which to push back against some of the beliefs on which social anxiety thrives: that we’re odd or different; that these things happen only to us; and that we’re to blame for both the occurrences themselves and the social anxiety that’s intertwined with them.

I want to end on some words by novelist Alice Walker, for she encapsulates the potential power of consciousness-raising rather well in writing that we must "resist the temptation to think what afflicts you is peculiar to you. Have faith that what is in your consciousness can be communicated to the consciousness of all. And is, in many cases, already there (1989).

Bates, Laura. (n.d.). Everyday Sexism Project

Butler, Gillian. (2016). Overcoming Social Anxiety and Shyness: A self-help guide using cognitive behavioural techniques. 2nd edition. London: Robinson.

Chamberlin, Judi. (2012 [1977]). On Our Own: Patient-controlled Alternatives to the Mental Health System. Lawrence, Massachusetts: National Empowerment Centre, Inc.

Masters, Katie. (2024). Feminist and Anti-psychiatry Perspectives on ‘Social Anxiety Disorder’: The Socially Anxious Woman. Cham: Palgrave Macmillan.

Office for National Statistics. (2026). Gender pay gap in the UK: 2026

Office for National Statistics. (2025). Sexual offences prevalence and victim characteristics, England and Wales

Sue, Derald Wing. (2010). Microaggressions in Everyday Life: Race, Gender, and Sexual Orientation. John Wiley and Sons.

Walker, Alice. (1989). The Temple of My Familiar. San Diego: Harcourt Brace Jovanovich.

Kia’s electric campervan, based on the PV5, includes two double beds, a 200 W solar panel, and a fully equipped kitchen.

The PV5, Kia’s first 100% electric van, has been a huge success for the Korean automaker. After launching it at the end of last year, the PV5 has already become Europe’s top-selling small (C-segment) electric van.

Based on its modular skateboard platform, called E-GMP.S, Kia can easily swap body styles to build custom configurations.

Although the PV5 is primarily sold in Passenger for everyday driving and Cargo for business use, Kia said the platform unlocks “endless possibilities” for different body styles and conversions, including a full-on electric campervan.

Wellhouse Leisure, a family-run campervan manufacturer based in the UK, revealed the Kia PV5 i-Camper.

The fully electric campervan is “now built and ready to view,” the company said. Based on the PV5 Cargo Plus, the campervan measures 4.69 m long, 1.89 m wide, and 1.99 m tall, which is about the size of a Ford Custom.

Although that’s pretty small for a camper, it offers more than you’d expect. Inside, the PV5 i-Camper includes two double beds with an elevating roof, a full kitchen setup, and a 200 W solar panel.

The sliding seat system enables the two rear seats to fold flat to form a bed and can be removed entirely. The upper bed, under the pop-up roof, has “more comfy” Froli Springs.

In the kitchen, you’ll find a sink with a tap and an electric water pump, two induction burners, a 42 L refrigerator, cabinets and storage spaces, and an optional microwave.

This EV would be a huge hit if imported into the US. Maybe after the huge order backlog has subsided Kia will consider importing the van to the States.

The vehicle also has a lithium leisure battery and a 12V supply, so you don’t need to use the vehicle’s main battery while camping.

It also comes with vehicle-to-load, letting you power external electrical devices, an e-bike, or even a campsite.

The PV5 Plus Long Range model uses a 71.2 kWh battery, providing a WLTP range of up to 247 miles. However, the added equipment will impact the range in the campervan conversion. Charging the battery from 10% to 80% takes around 30 minutes using a DC fast charger.

In the UK, Wellhouse Leisure lists the PV5 electric campervan starting at £63,000, or about $84,000.

#4805. I Have a New Hobby. It’s Kicking My Ass.

The fastest-growing racquet sport in America may also be the cardio workout I’ve been avoiding.

This column first appeared in the Men’s Health email newsletter. The Optimized Man is a biweekly series from our editorial director as he tries out the latest, greatest, and weirdest health and wellness innovations so you don’t have to. Sign up here to get the next one.

I’VE TRIED TO build a life free of shoulds. I’m fine with woulds and coulds and their vague promise of actionability, but when you get into shoulds, you get hung up on stuff like guilt and doubt and all kinds of second-guessing. I really should work out. I really shouldn’t eat that. You think I should try and sleep more? Thanks, man. Good tip.

Shoulds, put plainly, are a problem, and this year I’ve been staring down two different shoulds that won’t quit staring back: I should probably do more cardio, and I should probably get a hobby. I’ve never been much of a cardio guy or a hobby guy, but with evidence tying both to better physical and mental health outcomes, my list of excuses for not doing either is growing short. And I think I’ve found a solution in one of the fastest-growing sports in America.

It’s called padel (pronounced pa-DEL), and you might’ve come across it if you’ve been on vacation lately in Central America or southern Europe (or somewhere really exotic, like Miami). I discovered it last year on a cold winter’s night, and after playing for two hours on an indoor court and emerging sweaty, sore, and exuberant, I can report that it combines everything I like about tennis, racquetball, and squash into one hard-hitting, heavy-breathing sport.

You can go ahead and YouTube the basics, and here’s the gist: You’re playing on a court that’s about three-quarters the area of a tennis court, with high glass walls along the back, some wire fencing on the sides, and a net down the middle. Instead of pickleball’s slow and endless dinking, a padel ball whirs fast off your midsize racquet (also larger and heavier than pickleball’s), and the action requires you to move. Even though it’s a doubles sport (which typically requires less movement than singles, ‘cause there’s two of you), you’re constantly chasing the ball like it’s that little golden bug in quidditch. Sprint, stop, swing, pivot, repeat. (You can also hit the ball against the back wall to launch it in reverse, back over the net, which requires a massive swing.) The first time I played, I showed up wearing sweatpants and a puffer vest over a T-shirt. Within minutes of starting I had sweat through my T-shirt, and by the end of the first set, I had sweat through the seat of my sweatpants. I looked like John Candy in Splash, post-racquetball. What can I say? I’m not a cardio guy.

And there is a lot of cardio here. Back in 2024 we noticed that tennis had started billing itself as “the world’s healthiest sport,” and we asked writer Nick Pachelli to dig into the branding to see how much of it is hype. According to Nick:

Padel isn’t tennis and tennis isn’t padel, but I’ve been playing tennis for almost four decades, and I’ve never had my ass kicked quite as hard as when I played padel.

Then there is the social aspect of it—you’re part of a pair playing another pair, and whether you’re close friends or total strangers with your partner or opponents, at least you’re not bowling alone. Nick found that when longevity researchers study tennis…

Aerobic exercise, social connection and community, some light competition, and a lot of laughs: Could padel be my new hobby? Could it be my main source of cardio? Winter’s coming and the indoor courts are calling, and with visions of John Candy huffing and puffing in my head, I should probably start training.

Richard Dorment is the editorial director of Men’s Health and Women’s Health.

#4801. Switching from GLP-1 Injections to Wegovy Pill Shows Additional Weight Loss of 4.1%

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People with overweight or obesity who switch from an injectable GLP-1 medication to the Wegovy (semaglutide) pill may continue to lose weight, according to findings from the OCTANE study presented at the 2026 Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy.

The study is among the first real-world analyses to examine weight loss and treatment experiences among people who switched from an injectable weight loss medication to oral semaglutide (Wegovy).

However, while real-world studies like this can provide useful insights into how treatments work in everyday life, these findings do not prove that switching to the Wegovy pill caused the weight loss.

The results have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed scientific journal.

This was a retrospective cohort analysis evaluating weight change, treatment adherence, and patient satisfaction after people switched from injectable semaglutide (Wegovy) or tirzepatide (Zepbound) to oral semaglutide for weight management.

The study included a random sample of 194 adults with overweight or obesity and at least one obesity-related complication, such as hypertension, cardiovascular disease, obstructive sleep apnea, and dyslipidemia.

Participants had no history of diabetes or bariatric surgery and had an average baseline weight of 221.6 pounds (100.5 kg) and an average body mass index (BMI) of 34.5 kg/m2.

Participants switched from an injectable GLP-1 medication to oral semaglutide between January 5 and February 7, 2026. There was no requirement for how long they had used an injectable medication or how much weight they had lost before switching.

Participants were required to use oral semaglutide regularly for 3 months and self-report their weight within 30 days of starting treatment and again at the end of the study period.

After 3 months of taking oral semaglutide, participants had lost an average of 4.1% of their body weight, or 8.8 pounds.

At the 3-month mark, 2 in 5 participants (40.7%) had lost 5% or more of their body weight.

The proportion of participants with a BMI of 30 or greater also decreased by 21.6 percentage points, from 87.1% at baseline to 65.5% after 3 months.

Most participants (82.4%) reported at least one treatment improvement. Around 69% reported better-fitting clothes, and around 51% reported eating healthier.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Medical Director, Diabetes & Metabolic Center at University Hospitals, Cleveland, OH, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that, “These findings are encouraging because they suggest that some people can continue losing weight after switching to oral treatment.”

However, she also noted, “I would view this as promising early evidence supporting another treatment option, rather than proof that switching improves results.”

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, noted that because the oral medication is absorbed through the gastrointestinal tract, less of it reaches the bloodstream compared to the injectable form.

However, oral semaglutide can still be effective for weight loss.

“While studies show that the injectable form is more efficacious, current findings demonstrate that the oral version is also effective for weight loss,” said Ali.

Some people may prefer the oral form for ease of use and transportation because it does not require refrigeration. However, it must be taken in the morning on an empty stomach, followed by a 30-minute wait before eating, Ali told Healthline.

“Both formulations can cause gastrointestinal side effects, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation. Taking a pill does not eliminate those risks,” Hatipoglu said.

Hatipoglu also said factors to consider include how well your current treatment is working, side effects, your comfort with injections, your daily routine, cost, and insurance coverage.

She added that the decision should be made with a prescribing clinician, who can help plan the transition and monitor your response.

“Both options can be effective, so patients should discuss the risks and benefits of each with their provider. Ultimately, these medications are tools to support a healthier diet and lifestyle, and patients who make these fundamental changes achieve the best results,” said Ali.

#4799. How This Busy Dad Got Leaner and Stronger in 11 Weeks Without Losing Much Weight

Strength coach Gareth Sapstead shares how he helped a busy dad and business owner get leaner, build muscle, and reshape his physique.

Body recomposition is widely viewed as the holy grail of physical transformation: losing body fat while simultaneously adding lean muscle.

It’s also often dismissed as either impossible or reserved exclusively for complete beginners. The logic appears fairly convincing. To lose fat, you need to consume fewer calories than you burn. To build muscle, you need enough energy to construct new tissue. One requires a deficit, the other seemingly demands a surplus.

Pick a lane: bulk first, cut later. Right?

Strength and physique coach Gareth Sapstead disagrees. In a detailed breakdown published on his website, Sapstead explains how he helped father and business owner Mark Schadenberg transform his physique ahead of a Men’s Health Netherlands photoshoot—losing fat, adding visible muscle and finishing just 4 pounds lighter after 11 weeks.

The scales barely budged, but his body changed dramatically.

“The fitness industry has been telling you to pick one for decades,” says Sapstead. “Bulk first, cut later. Build the muscle, then reveal it.”

Sapstead accepts that fat loss requires an energy deficit, while building muscle requires energy. However, he says the apparent contradiction comes from treating your body like a single energy account.

“Fat tissue and muscle tissue operate through different pathways,” he explains. “You can be breaking down stored fat for fuel while simultaneously building muscle protein—as long as the conditions for muscle protein synthesis are met.”

Those conditions are relatively straightforward: enough protein and a sufficiently challenging resistance-training stimulus.

Sapstead points towards research examining simultaneous fat loss and muscle gain. According to Sapstead, the phenomenon appeared consistently across the research and wasn’t simply a beginner-only fluke.

He also references studies in which participants consumed between 400 and 800 additional calories each day, all from protein.

By conventional logic, those extra calories should have resulted in weight gain. Instead, Sapstead says the participants either maintained their weight or lost fat while gaining or preserving muscle.

“Body recomposition is real,” he concludes. “It’s well-supported, and for the right person in the right circumstances, it happens faster than most expect.”

Schadenberg had just 11 weeks to prepare for his photoshoot. He was running a business and raising a family—a familiar combination for many of us—that had gradually pushed training, nutrition, and recovery down his list of priorities.

“He’d let his training slip,” says Sapstead. “Not from a lack of drive, but through the entirely predictable reality of running a business and raising a family.”

His sleep was suffering, his diet lacked structure and he had no consistent exercise routine. Like many men in their late 30s and 40s, Sapstead says, he was also “chronically undereating protein.”

That might not sound like an ideal starting point, but it gave Schadenberg several powerful variables to improve almost immediately.

“Every one of those factors is a recomposition accelerant,” says Sapstead.

Returning to resistance training after a significant lay-off can produce a response closer to that of a beginner. The stimulus feels novel again, adaptations arrive quickly and previously built muscle may return faster than it took to develop in the first place.

Combine that with more protein, better recovery and structured training, and you can create the conditions to rebuild muscle while using stored body fat to help cover the energy costs.

“The body has been starved of the right inputs,” says Sapstead. “Give it protein, training and adequate recovery, and it responds.”

After 11 weeks, Schadenberg was only 4 pounds lighter. But his before-and-after photographs showed considerably more muscle and significantly less body fat.

“Fat came off. Muscle went on. Bodyweight barely moved,” says Sapstead.

Sapstead says recomposition is particularly well suited to anyone who has been away from consistent strength training, is carrying more body fat than they would like, habitually eats too little protein or has allowed sleep and recovery to deteriorate.

For experienced lifters who have trained intelligently, eaten well, and slept properly for years, the process is likely to be slower. There’s simply less low-hanging fruit.

For returning lifters, however, they're in a prime position for a recomp.

This isn’t the time for an aggressive diet or an uncontrolled bulk. Sapstead recommends eating around your maintenance calories or slightly above them, with approximately 200 to 300 additional calories coming predominantly from protein.

The aim is to provide enough energy to support training and muscle growth without creating a large surplus that encourages unnecessary fat gain.

Sapstead sets protein at around one gram per pound of bodyweight as a starting point, although higher intakes may also be appropriate.

Protein provides the raw materials required to repair and construct muscle tissue. It is also highly satiating, making it easier to control your overall food intake without constantly feeling hungry.

Perform three to four structured resistance-training sessions each week, with a focus on progressive overload.

Your body needs a reason to preserve and build muscle. That means gradually adding weight, completing more reps, improving your range of motion or producing better-quality work—not simply getting hot and tired doing random circuits, or going through the motions with zero intensity.

When fat is coming off while muscle is being added, your bodyweight may barely change. That doesn’t mean the approach has stopped working. It may mean it’s working exactly as intended.

“The scale would have told him nothing was happening,” Sapstead says of Schadenberg’s transformation. “The photos would have told him everything.”

Take progress pictures every two to three weeks, track your gym performance and pay attention to how your clothes fit. If your waist is shrinking, your strength is improving and you look more muscular, a stable bodyweight isn’t failure—it’s the holy grail of body recomp in action.

#4798. Why Is It So Easy to Feel Depressed?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 7, 2026 | Reviewed by Lybi Ma

Everyone knows, or will likely know one day, what it feels like to be depressed. This is why depression is often referred to as "the common cold of mental illness." This reference reveals some fundamental insights into why we also become depressed when we are suffering from the flu or a bacterial infection. Bacteria induce our bodies to release an ancient form of chemical warfare called cytokines. These cytokines are part of our immune system's defensive arsenal, protecting us from invading bacteria or viruses. When we get sick, we engage in sickness behaviors: we remove ourselves from company and become less active while our bodies try to heal. When your dog is sick, it might hide under the bed and sleep for days, not even eating.

Humans do the same thing. When a person feels depressed, they demonstrate many of the same symptoms. For the past few decades, depression was thought to be caused by dysfunction of serotonin neurons. Neuroscientists now understand that this was due to our ignorance about the nature of depression. Depression-like behaviors are now thought to be caused by the release of cytokines into the body and brain [for more about this topic, see: The Brain: What Everyone Needs to Know]. Depression may be so common because the condition initially evolved to help us survive infections and be healthy (Dantzer, 2009)

Sickness behaviors help our survival. Sometimes, however, cytokines and other pro-inflammatory chemicals can be released inappropriately and for prolonged periods, leading to sickness behaviors that last too long. Many recent scientific studies have shown that cytokine-induced processes are active in our brain during depression. A few years ago, it was discovered that standard antidepressant medications exhibit anti-inflammatory actions that can counteract the depressive effects of cytokines. This insight may also explain why these medications are often less effective in obese individuals because their brains demonstrate quite elevated levels of inflammation.

The incidence of depression in the US is almost as high as the incidence of obesity. Considerable evidence indicates that the two conditions are related. Studies indicate that individuals with obesity have a 32 percent higher risk of developing depression compared to those with normal weight; depressed individuals are also more likely to become obese over time. Obesity increases the risk of depression, and depression similarly predicts future obesity, highlighting a reciprocal association.

Researchers have explored mechanisms underlying the link between the two conditions. Elevated leptin, primarily produced by fat cells, is consistently associated with more depressive symptoms, while adiponectin typically exhibits a negative correlation (Labad and colleagues, 2012). Leptin has become a possible target for novel therapeutic approaches to the treatment of depression (Tongtong and colleagues, 2018). In addition, pro-inflammatory proteins released by fat cells travel to the brain and reduce neurogenesis inside the hippocampus. Reduced neurogenesis strongly correlates with depression; restoration of neurogenesis is associated with improved mood.

Physicians regularly encourage their depressed patients to lose weight. Studies have shown that calorie‑restricted diets reduce depressive symptoms in obese patients. A systematic review found that most weight‑loss dietary interventions lead to decreased depression scores (Patsalos and colleagues, 2021).

Depression is so common because inflammation related to obesity or illness is so common. Our currently available antidepressant medications exhibit modest anti-inflammatory effects through diverse mechanisms, such as reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines or enhancing anti-inflammatory cytokines within specific brain regions that play a role in depression (Bleibel and colleagues, 2025). Future antidepressant therapies will no longer focus on serotonin, norepinephrine, or dopamine; rather, research is now focused on drugs that reduce brain inflammation. These newer drugs will likely be far more effective than the popular ones of the last half-century.

Dantzer R (2009) Cytokine, Sickness Behavior, and Depression. Immunol Allergy Clin North Am. 29(2):247–264. doi: 10.1016/j.iac.2009.02.002

Labad J et al., (2012) Leptin levels and depressive symptoms in people with Type 2 diabetes: the Edinburgh Type 2 diabetes study. Biopsychosocial Science and Medicine 74, 39–45

Tongtong G, et al., (2018) Leptin in depression: a potential therapeutic target. Cell Death Dis. 26;9(11):1096. doi: 10.1038/s41419-018-1129-1 PMCID: PMC6203758 PMID: 30367065

Patsalos O, et al., (2021) Diet, Obesity, and Depression: A Systematic Review. J. Pers. Med., 11(3), 176; https://doi.org/10.3390/jpm11030176

Bleibel L, et al., (2025) Unveiling the anti-inflammatory effects of antidepressants: a systematic review of human studies over the last decade. Pharmaceuticals, 18(6), 867; https://doi.org/10.3390/ph18060867

#4796. Volkswagen’s EV battery recall reaches over 85,000, with Audi now included

Volkswagen’s latest recall now extends to Audi, affecting nearly 13,000 Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles globally. And just like with the ID.4, owners are being told to limit charging to 80% of the battery’s capacity.

Earlier this month, Volkswagen issued a recall with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) impacting 22,524 ID.4 electric SUVs, model years 2023 to 2026.

Official information from the German Federal Motor Transport Authority (KBA) revealed shortly after that several thousand more VW Group electric vehicles are affected worldwide.

In three separate recalls now under investigation by the KBA, 72,668 VW Group EVs were included worldwide, including 9,881 in Germany.

The recall affects certain batches of the ID. Buzz, ID.3, ID.4, and ID.7 models produced between 2022 and 2025, as well as Cupra Born models from 2022 to 2024.

On October 27, VW Group added another electric vehicle to the KBA recall database. The latest recall impacts 12,734 Audi Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles globally, including just one in Germany. In total, Volkswagen’s battery recall now affects 85,402 EVs globally.

In the letter sent to the NHTSA on October 23, Volkswagen Group of America said it was issuing a recall affecting 9,048 Audi Q4 E-Tron and Q4 Sportback E-Tron vehicles in the US model years 2024 to 2025.

The recall stems from the risk of the battery overheating and potentially causing a fire under certain conditions when charged to over 80% of its limit.

Volkswagen said in a safety recall report with the NHTSA that “certain charging profiles combined with a state of charge over 80% may trigger thermal propagation.”

While the root cause is unknown, Volkswagen urged owners to limit charging to 80%. Owners of affected vehicles received an email saying VW “intends to apply a temporary vehicle setting that limits charging to 80%,” unless they opted out by October 21.

The safety recall follows Audi’s Product Safety Committee being informed of battery thermal events involving other Volkswagen Group EVs that use the same batteries as the Audi Q4 E-Tron.

Following an internal investigation, Audi found the same battery and production characteristics as the impacted VW Group vehicles. Audi said the majority of these were produced for the North American market.

Audi is not aware of any claims, crashes, fires, injuries, or deaths associated with the Q4 E-Tron’s battery issue.

Dang it. I posted this concern in the other article that covered the ID.4 that Audi Q4 would be next. And here we are. I guess I'm going to have to call the hotline and see if mine is part of the recall. This is starting out just like the Chevy Bolt fiasco. I had a 2020 Bolt that eventually got a new battery pack but it was a battle with GM till they finally got it done. My guess is the VW group will do the same thing here. And oh by the way selling the car while this recall is in question will be a no go. Ugghh.

The root cause has yet to be determined, and until a remedy is available, Audi is advising owners to limit charging to 80%.

Owners in the US can take their vehicles to an authorized Audi dealer, where the dealer will run a diagnostic check on the battery. If needed, the dealer will impose a temporary state-of-charge limit to 80%.

Audi expects to mail out interim letters notifying owners of the safety risks on December 18, 2026. Additional letters will send additional letters once a remedy is available.

Owners can contact Audi’s customer service at 1-800-253-2834 with questions or concerns. Audi’s recall number is 93SK. You can also contact the NHTSA Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit nhtsa.gov for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V698.

#4795. Detached Nails More Than 4 Times Higher Among GLP-1 Users, Study Finds

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

GLP-1 users have reported various unusual side effects like “Ozempic feet,” “Ozempic butt,” and “Ozempic breasts.” These changes have been largely tied to rapid weight loss.

Now, fingernails have entered the conversation. Nails detaching from the nail bed or changing color may be more common among people taking GLP-1 drugs, according to a new study. In the study, which researchers presented in October at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) Congress 2026 in Vienna, people taking GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide — Ozempic, Wegovy — and tirzepatide — Mounjaro, Zepbound — reported nail detachment and nail discoloration more often than people who didn’t take the drugs.

When the researchers counted only nail changes that started after treatment began, the link between GLP-1 use and nail detachment nearly disappeared, study author Charles Taïeb, MD, PhD, told Healthline.

“This is why we insist that a substantial part of the nail excess reflects the patients’ overall health rather than the drug itself, while a modest drug-specific effect remains plausible,” Taïeb said.Earlier research has also linked GLP-1 use to hair loss. In the new study, the researchers explained why they examined nails, noting that nails and hair both grow from cells that divide quickly.

However, the researchers cautioned in a press release that the study can’t establish that the drugs caused the nail changes. Both the nail study and a companion hair study captured self-reported symptoms at a single point in time, a design that can identify associations only, they said.

For the study, researchers examined a representative sample of people in France, the United States, Brazil, and Mexico.

Participants included 575 people taking GLP-1 drugs and 1,329 people with type 2 diabetes, obesity, or both conditions, who had never taken GLP-1 drugs.

The average treatment duration was 18.5 months, and researchers tracked weight loss over three months.

They also looked separately at people who had lost weight, to help tell whether the drugs or the weight loss explained the changes. However, the abstract didn’t specify which GLP-1 drugs participants took.

The researchers have submitted the findings to peer-reviewed dermatology journals, where they are under review, Taïeb told Healthline. Here’s what they found.

According to the American Academy of Dermatology (AAD), nail detachment, or onycholysis, occurs when a nail lifts, and the lifted area often appears white.

Taïeb told Healthline that the study asked about “nail detachment” because patients, not doctors, filled out the questionnaire. Nail detachment was the strongest signal among the five nail changes the researchers asked about, Taïeb said.

According to the abstract, 39% of GLP-1 users reported nail separation or detachment (onycholysis), compared with 9% of nonusers.

Nail discoloration is a change in a nail’s usual color, such as white, yellow, or greenish-black, according to the AAD.According to the abstract, 46% of GLP-1 users reported discoloration, compared with 17% of nonusers. Ridges or grooves and fragile nails were also more common among GLP-1 users.

Mir B. Ali, MD, a bariatric surgeon and medical director of the MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Los Angeles, said that while he prescribes GLP-1s, nail detachment hasn’t come up in his practice. Ali wasn’t involved in the research.“I haven’t had anybody complain of that. It’s not something we really see,” he told Healthline. He said his patients more often mention brittle nails or minor changes in nail color.

Over a three-month period, 76% of GLP-1 users reported weight loss, compared with 47% of nonusers, according to the abstract.Weight loss alone didn’t appear to explain the nail findings, the researchers said in the press release. The differences between users and nonusers held up when they looked only at people who had lost weight.The researchers also cautioned in the press release that the study can’t show the drugs caused the changes. They noted that about half of GLP-1 users had nail problems before starting treatment.

Adjusting for skin conditions and nutritional deficiencies weakened some of the associations, they said, though nail detachment and discoloration stayed about two to three times as common among users.Those adjustments relied on conditions participants reported, including iron, vitamin B12, zinc, and vitamin D deficiencies, as well as psoriasis, eczema, and other skin conditions, Taïeb said.“GLP-1 medications may affect the nails indirectly rather than directly,” said Tanya Evans, MD, a board certified dermatologist and medical director of the Skin Cancer Program at the Melanoma Clinic at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA, who wasn’t involved in the research.Because the drugs reduce appetite, some people may eat less protein, iron, and zinc, which can contribute to brittle nails, discoloration, or nail detachment, Evans told Healthline. Rapid weight loss may also temporarily disrupt nail growth, much as it can trigger hair shedding, she said.Ali said the total amount of weight a person loses plays a bigger role in hair and nail changes than the rate at which they lose it.

The U.S. labels for Wegovy and Zepbound list hair loss as a side effect reported in clinical trials.

The labels for the Ozempic, both injectable and pill form, as well as Mounjaro, list hair loss as a side effect, based on reports received after the drugs entered the market. Those reports don’t establish how often it happens or whether the drugs caused it.

As such, researchers have been examining GLP-1-related hair loss.

A companion study of the same participants found hair and scalp changes were also more common among GLP-1 users, according to that study’s abstract, also provided to Healthline:

Scalp redness was about three times as common among users, and most users with hair loss also had scalp symptoms such as itching, redness, or scaling.Scalp inflammation may play a role in hair changes among GLP-1 users, in addition to the shedding that often follows rapid weight loss, one of the study’s authors stated in the news release.“This raises the possibility that inflammation may be contributing in some patients, rather than the problem being solely the classic temporary hair shedding associated with rapid weight loss,” Evans said.Experts have told Healthline that hair loss on GLP-1 drugs is often temporary and tied to weight loss.“Hair loss, we see commonly, not only in patients who are on GLP-1 medications, but also in our surgical weight loss patients,” Ali said.

“When you lose weight, especially in women, it releases hormones. You’re getting metabolic changes, and all these things can lead to hair loss and some changes in the nails.” Ali said he tells patients that “as the weight stabilizes at a healthy weight, the hormones stabilize and the hair tends to come back to where it was before.”

Nail detachment and discoloration don’t appear as adverse reactions in the current U.S. prescribing information for Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, or Zepbound.

Ali said the best thing patients can do is get the right nutrition, including enough protein. He said he also advises patients to take a multivitamin along with B-complex, vitamin D, and calcium.

“I would not recommend stopping the GLP-1 medication simply because nail detachment occurs,” Evans said. She advised people to tell their doctor about any new changes in hair, scalp, or nails.Treatment for nail detachment or discoloration depends on the cause, Evans said. A dermatologist can check for an infection, an inflammatory nail disorder, a nutritional problem, an injury, or another explanation, she said.A detached nail recovers as a new nail grows out from its base, Evans said. That takes about 4 to 6 months for a fingernail and 9 to 12 months for a toenail.

Lastly, the AAD recommends having a board certified dermatologist examine any nail that’s lifting.

The AAD also recommends seeing a dermatologist if skin, hair, or nail side effects don’t improve, as they can help determine whether symptoms are due to the medication or another condition.“The important message is don’t panic, but don’t ignore persistent nail changes either,” Evans said.

#4794. Dems introduce new $15,000 EV tax credit bill that has no chance — and that’s a problem

Rep. Greg Landsman (D-OH) wants to bring back the federal EV tax credit and double it. His new bill, the “21st Century Vehicle Choice Act” (H.R. 10881), would offer up to $15,000 on a new electric vehicle and $8,000 on a used one, and it would make both credits permanent.

The problem is that the bill has virtually no chance of becoming law anytime soon. And if EV shoppers start holding out for it, it could end up hurting the market it’s trying to help.

Landsman introduced H.R. 10881 on October 22. It was referred to three House committees (Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Natural Resources), and as of today, it doesn’t have a single cosponsor.

The big change is to the new clean vehicle credit, Section 30D of the tax code. Under the Inflation Reduction Act, the $7,500 credit came in two $3,750 halves: one for meeting critical mineral sourcing requirements and one for battery components. Landsman’s bill doubles each half to $7,500, for a maximum of $15,000.

It also deletes the termination dates. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act killed the new and used EV credits for vehicles acquired after September 30, 2025, and the home charger credit after June 30, 2026. Striking those dates would revive all three credits with no expiration.

The bill doesn’t touch the rest of 30D. North American final assembly, the $55,000 MSRP cap on cars and $80,000 cap on SUVs, pickups, and vans, and the foreign entity of concern rules all stay. So the full $15,000 would only go to EVs that clear both sourcing tests, which has always been a short list.

The rest of the bill is reports. Commerce would deliver a “Vehicle Choice Report” on vehicle variety and ownership costs, and the Department of Energy would file five years of critical minerals reports.

The most interesting part is a DOE study of “gasoline super-users,” defined as the top 10% of light-duty vehicle owners by gas consumption. The study would map the regions where they’re concentrated and their 100 most-used routes, then track charger availability along those routes every year for five years. Coltura, which backs the bill, says the highest-mileage drivers spend over 10% of household income on fuel.

Republicans control both the House and the Senate, and they’re the ones who just repealed these credits. President Trump signed that repeal.

Even if Democrats flip the House and Senate in next week’s midterms, a bill restoring EV credits would still need to get through a veto. So realistically, nothing like this happens before 2029.

It’s also a rerun. Landsman introduced the exact same “21st Century Vehicle Choice Act” as H.R. 10046 on October 25, 2024, 11 days before that year’s election. It got zero cosponsors and died in committee. This version landed 12 days before the November 3 midterms.

This is where the bill can do real damage. EV buyers are extremely sensitive to tax credit timing, and the last year proved it.

When the credit was about to disappear, buyers rushed in, and Q3 2025 became the best quarter ever for US EV sales, with market share topping 10% for the first time. Then the floor dropped out. Hyundai’s Ioniq 5 sales fell 63% the month after the credit ended.

The market is only now crawling back. According to Cox Automotive, US EV sales hit 262,649 units in Q3 2026, up 6.1% from Q2 but still down 39.5% year-over-year, at a 6.4% share of new vehicle sales. Tesla’s Model Y and Model 3 still dominate, but Toyota, Rivian, and Hyundai are growing again.

That recovery is fragile. A headline promising “$15,000 off your next EV” is exactly what makes a shopper on the fence decide to wait a year or two.

And waiting gets you nothing. The new credits would only apply to vehicles placed in service after the bill is enacted, so there’s no retroactive payout for buying now. If you already claimed the credit once, you’d get $0 anyway.

Meanwhile, the deals on the lot are real. Automakers have been cutting prices to make up for the lost credit, like Hyundai, which cut the 2026 Ioniq 5 by nearly $10,000 on some trims.

At Electrek, our position has always been clear: we think EVs are a net positive and ICE vehicles have unpriced externalities. Therefore, we will take whatever we can get to encourage EV sales, but our preferred approach would be a carbon tax on ICE vehicles.

We’ve been clear that policy shapes this market. Killing the $7,500 credit is the main reason US EV sales collapsed. Consumers didn’t suddenly decide they hate EVs. So we’re all for bringing incentives back.

But this bill is messaging. It has zero cosponsors and no CBO score, and it dropped two weeks before an election, just like the identical version two years ago.

They should focus on rooftop and community solar tax credits and initiatives. With rising electric rates, helping people alleviate those would be vastly more popular than EV subsidies.

To be fair, some of it is smart. The lower income caps and the once-per-taxpayer limit go after the most common criticism of the old credit, that it subsidized wealthy households buying their second or third EV. And the “super-user” study is the best idea in the bill. Getting a high-mileage driver out of a gas pickup does far more for fuel costs and emissions than putting a low-mileage commuter in their second Tesla. If Democrats want to rebuild EV policy in 2029, that’s where they should start.

The problem is that people will hear the headline number. If you need a car now and an EV fits your life, buy it now and take the deals that are on the table. Don’t plan your purchase around a bill that has no path to passing for at least two years.

Will Democrats come back with a real, cosponsored EV plan before 2028? I don’t know, but I suspect that the US will continue to fall behind the rest of the world when it comes to EV adoption.

If you’re buying an EV, powering it with home solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero, with or without a tax credit. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4793. Used EVs are suddenly hot sellers — Here are the top SUVs for under $25,000

Don’t want to pay full price? Used EVs with low miles, like the Hyundai IONIQ 5 and Ford Mustang Mach-E, are selling on the secondhand market for $25,000 or less.

With a flood of electric cars returning from lease this year and soaring gas prices, used EVs are suddenly flying off the lot.

Used EV sales rose to a record 3.3% of total used vehicle sales last month, up from 2.9% in August, according to Cox Automotive.

Used ICE vehicle sales, on the other hand, dropped 4.4% in September as buyers flocked to more efficient options.

As expected, Tesla remains the leading used EV brand, followed by Ford, Chevrolet, Hyundai, and BMW.

By model, the Nissan Ariya led growth, with sales up 42.5% in September, followed by the Chevy Equinox EV (+41.9%), Kia EV9 (+36.2%), and Chevy Blazer EV (+30.2%), while the Ford Mustang Mach-E (+14.7%) and Tesla Model Y (+13.8 %) also saw more demand.

With more options to choose from, which one is best for you? To help you decide, Edmunds, which has tested nearly all of them, put together a list of four top used electric SUVs available for under $25,000.

The first one on the list was the Chevy Equinox EV, or as GM used to call it, “America’s most affordable 315+ range” electric vehicle.

After it arrived in 2024, the Chevy Equinox EV quickly became one of the top-selling electric vehicles in the US outside Tesla, winning over buyers with enough space for a family and plenty of driving range at an affordable price.

The Chevy Equinox EV offers up to 319 miles of EPA-estimated driving range. It’s a great fit for those looking for a smaller, more efficient SUV that still offers plenty of interior space.

Edmunds says it’s worth upgrading to the 2LT trim, which adds heated front seats and a heated steering wheel, a wireless phone charger, adaptive cruise control, and a 360-degree HD Surround Vision camera system.

Next on the list was the Ford Mustang Mach-E, which has also remained a top seller since it went on sale in 2021.

Ford tapped into its iconic Mustang nameplate to help attract new buyers. The Mustang Mach-E came well equipped with a large 15.5″ infotainment screen with Wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto and Ford Co-Pilot360 Assist+.

While the GT is the most fun to drive, Edmunds said the Premium trim may be your best bet. It still offers plenty of performance while adding standard features like heated front seats and a heated steering wheel.

It’s also worth upgrading to the extended-range battery pack, which offers up to 320 miles of range on the Premium RWD model. You should be able to find used 2021 to 2023 Mach-E’s for under $25,000.

Another top-selling electric SUV, the Hyundai IONIQ 5 continues to win over buyers with its bold design, long-range capabilities, fast charging, and a surprisingly spacious interior.

Edmunds says plenty of used 2022 to 2024 IONIQ 5s with low mileage are available for under $25,000.

While the base SE Standard Range is the cheapest, it only offers an EPA range of 220 miles. Upgrading to the Extended Range battery, which is used on all other trims, provides up to 303 miles of range.

The Volkswagen ID.4 went on sale in the US in 2021 as one of the earlier mainstream electric SUVs.

It also just happens that many EVs are coming off lease so the inventory is plentiful combined with high gas price. Perfect storm.

It was updated in 2024, but up until the 2023 model year, the VW ID.4 offered an EPA range of up to 275 miles, depending on the configuration.

Finding a low-mileage used 2023 ID.4 shouldn’t be hard, but upgrading to the Pro S trim might be worth it.

Volkswagen updated the 2023 ID.4 with a new 12″ infotainment display and Park Assist Plus. The Pro S trim gained a fixed panoramic roof, V-Tex synthetic leather seating, and a heated steering wheel.

#4792. Pain Prevalence Higher in Women, Increases Most Rapidly Before 55

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Women experience a higher prevalence of pain than men across different areas of the body, according to a large global study published October 5 in Nature Medicine.

The analysis, which included more than 6 million people, also found that pain prevalence generally increased with age, with the most rapid increases occurring before age 55.

The findings come as lower back pain, neck pain, and osteoarthritis — all common causes of pain — are projected to become more prevalent globally by 2050.

Pain, especially lower back pain, is the leading cause of disability worldwide. However, researchers have lacked a standardized way to examine how self-reported pain varies across the life span and different regions of the world.

This new study is one of the largest efforts to date to examine self-reported pain using a standardized approach.

The researchers analyzed data from 6,125,459 individuals spanning 118 countries from 1990 to 2025. Participants ranged in age from 5 to more than 100, and 55% were female.

They used self-reported data on pain across 11 body sites:

The researchers found that women consistently reported a higher prevalence of pain across all 11 sites than men.

The largest differences between women and men were in facial pain, headache, and stomach or abdominal pain.

Pain prevalence also increased most rapidly before age 55, especially at musculoskeletal sites such as the hips, back, and knees.

The researchers found that the prevalence of pain varied considerably by body region and differed by age.

Back pain was the most commonly reported, affecting 40% of participants, while facial pain was the least common at 2%.

Neel Anand, MD, a board certified orthopedic spine surgeon and director of the Cedars-Sinai Spine Center in Los Angeles, who wasn’t involved in the study, explained some factors that may contribute to the high prevalence of back pain.

“Our modern lifestyles involve more prolonged sitting, less physical activity, and more time spent looking down at phones, tablets, and computers, all of which can contribute to poor posture and increased stress on the spine,” he said.

“As we get older, the discs between our vertebrae naturally lose moisture and elasticity, making them more vulnerable to degeneration, bulging, and herniation. Excess weight and smoking can accelerate this process,” Anand added.

In addition to pain at individual body sites, the researchers examined three broader measures: any bodily pain, high intensity pain, and generalized pain.

Any bodily pain was defined as pain reported at any site. High intensity pain was defined as an average pain intensity of 7 or higher on a 0–10 scale. Generalized pain was defined as pain occurring in 4 of 5 body regions according to the 2016 fibromyalgia spatial criteria.

The prevalence of any bodily pain increased progressively across the life span, from around 30% at age 5 to 70% among people ages 100 and older. All three pain measures were consistently higher in women than men.

While any bodily pain increased with age, high intensity and generalized pain peaked in mid-to-late life before declining.

High intensity pain peaked around age 50, while generalized pain peaked around age 70.

These different patterns could help identify when prevention and pain management efforts may be most beneficial across the life span.

Vernon Williams, MD, a sports neurologist and founding director of the Center for Sports Neurology and Pain Medicine at Cedars-Sinai Orthopedics and Sports Medicine in Los Angeles, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline there are several signs that pain should be evaluated by a doctor.

“People shouldn’t feel that they simply have to live with pain. I especially recommend talking with a doctor when pain persists, interferes with sleep or daily activities, limits exercise or function, or is accompanied by symptoms such as numbness, tingling, or weakness,” Williams said.

“Persistent pain deserves an evaluation to identify the underlying cause and develop an appropriate treatment plan.”

The researchers found that smoking, obesity, and lower household income together accounted for 18.3% of the global pain burden across all body sites.

People who currently smoked had a modest but consistently higher prevalence of pain across body sites from adolescence through age 65. The strongest association was seen with facial pain.

Obesity was increasingly associated with pain beginning in early adulthood, particularly in weight-bearing joints such as the knees, hips, feet, and ankles.

Lower household income was also associated with a higher prevalence of pain across all body sites beginning in early adulthood. The strongest association was seen with chest pain.

People with the lowest household incomes were more than twice as likely to report chest pain as those with the highest incomes. This difference was greatest in midlife and narrowed at older ages.

Williams noted that medication isn’t the only option for managing pain.

“Regular, appropriately paced exercise can help change how the brain experiences pain, while mindfulness, breathing exercises, adequate sleep, and other behavioral strategies can help the nervous system better regulate the pain response,” he said. “When medication is needed, I encourage patients to discuss non-opioid and non-pharmacologic options with their doctor as part of a comprehensive approach.”

Anand added that, “The best strategy remains prevention and preservation of function: maintaining a healthy weight, strengthening the muscles that support the joints, and avoiding smoking can all help reduce the strain placed on the musculoskeletal system.”

#4791. Dutch startup Elysian says electric flight may be closer than you think

They day you get to book an all-electric flight may be closer than you think if Dutch startup Elysian Aircraft gets its way. Their new E9X commercial airliner promises flights that are a whole lot quieter, and at prices that are whole lot less dependent on dumb oil wars.

Aircraft account for more than 2% of global heating when CO₂ and other emissions are taken into account, with the share considerably higher in wealthy countries, according to data cited by climate campaign group Stay Grounded. Elysian Aircraft is keenly aware of the industry’s climate impact, and they believe their planned full-size electric airliner will be perfectly positioned to make a dramatic difference.

“By being able to transport 90 passengers for initially 800 kilometers and eventually 1,000 kilometers you can reduce emissions to zero, from half the world’s flights,” Elysian co-founder Daniel Jacobson told EuroNews. “That is a very large amount of flight activity in the world. And you reduce total emissions from aerospace by 20%.”

At the core of those ambitious emission-reduction goals is the Elysian E9X aircraft. Designed in collaboration with aerospace researchers at Delft University of Technology (TU Delft), the E9X packs its oversized wings with modular battery packs, sending power to six propellers driven by electric motors.

Specs on those haven’t been revealed, but the E9X is designed to carry up to 100 passengers up to 1,000 km (~620 miles) from where they started. Elysian says that’s enough range to handle nearly 50% of scheduled commercial passenger flights worldwide and potentially eliminate 20% of total in-flight emissions when the plane enters service in 2034.

That said, the E9X is far more than “just a concept,” and Elysian has completed its second conceptual design review and flown a scaled demonstrator in concert with Germany’s DLR aerospace research center, demonstrating how its unique battery packaging solutions address the challenges of integrating heavy battery packs into an aircraft’s wings (where fuel is traditionally stored).

It’s interesting to see all the comments that point out the difficulties and problems associated with the introduction of battery powered aircraft into the mainstream industry. What none of them address is the industry’s obsession with cutting their operating costs no matter what pain passengers and flight crews must endure. My bet is if the airlines can save money by converting to battery powered aircraft—there are NO obstacles that will stop them from doing it. Battery electric aircraft may reduce operating costs by thousands of dollars per flight. That alone tells me that they will be flying passengers as soon as possible.

The company is also working with airline partners KLM and Transavia to explore the operational and commercial requirements for putting electric airliners into service, with aircraft lessor TrueNoord investigating how the E9X could be financed and supported commercially.

#4790. 5 Simple Habits of People Who Naturally Feel Confident

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 7, 2026 | Reviewed by Margaret Foley

Truly confident people don't let life (or anyone else) run the show.

One way you can learn to take back control when life feels off-kilter is by practicing self-care. But self-care involves more than most people realize. It's a combination of physical and mental steps, like positive thinking, that help you feel like you're in balance and in control of your life.

But holding on to your self-care practice is hard when life starts to tip out of control—you know, those weeks that are especially challenging, when the days seem endless, and all you can do is make it to Friday night?

When life feels overwhelming, it's easy to wonder if you can handle it. That's especially true when you feel like you're trying hard to hold on to balance and don't want to lose your footing. This balancing act can seem almost impossible when life gets volatile. We all need support and encouragement, and sometimes even a mindset overhaul to stay in control and maintain our power.

Holding on to confidence amid uncertainty can feel like a superpower, one that can feel elusive and hard to reach. My experience is that this form of self-care is a hidden cornerstone found in all confident people's lives.

1. They tell themself they can handle this.

First of all, even if you think you can’t, you can handle this. Try using the mantra of “I can handle this” when doubt strikes. The anxiety you're feeling is likely a signal for needed growth. And even when that is true, it's also true that you're still handling the moment you're in now. Recognizing that you're coping, even if it isn’t graceful, is important.

2. They are careful where they pin their expectations.

In the spirit of making stress as low as possible, limit high expectations in general, or in any situation that tempts you to get your heart set on something over which you have limited control.

Your hopes and dreams are precious commodities—be protective of them and take care not to put them at unnecessary risk. Focus on realistic goals, informed by what is actually happening. Notice where you feel traction, and aim to build expectations from there.

Research shows that people with strong self-efficacy are more motivated and persistent when faced with obstacles, as they believe their efforts will ultimately pay off. Focusing expectations on what they can achieve through their own actions strengthens this internal motivation.

Even when you're keeping expectations in check, disappointments will still happen, and no matter how small these setbacks are, they can still hurt. It hurts because you care.

It’s OK to care, and it’s OK to be sad for a short while before moving forward. Life is a journey, and like any journey, pace is critical. Do your best to keep moving so you don’t get stuck on any one step or disappointment along the way.

Acknowledging disappointment prevents it from festering and evolving into more damaging emotions, according to one study. Empowered individuals recognize that letting go of a disappointing experience is beneficial for their long-term well-being and prevents unnecessary stress.

Your self-care can help keep you connected to a sense of balance in your life, especially during times of higher stress. That is the time when self-care is so sorely needed, which is, of course, when it can seem harder to do than you'd like.

How are you sleeping? How is your nutrition? Are you hydrating and being mindful of caffeine or alcohol intake? Are you moving your body at all? Are power naps or power walking crossing your radar? Look to realign places that are out of balance to help boost your stamina. Not pressure, just gentle nudges.

Self-care is like a muscle that gets stronger with regular practice, improving overall self-control and the ability to override habitual responses, one study concluded. Genuine self-care involves being kind to yourself, recognizing imperfections, and avoiding self-criticism, which can lead to better outcomes.

5. They identify how they're overextending and pull back.

When stress rears its head, you might end up stretching to meet its demands. This is how you grow and get stronger. But when you stretch too much and avoid setting limits, especially at work, you risk a diminishing return on engagement. Focusing on perfection can make you feel out of balance and less happy as well.

Saying no can be tough, though. If you're overextending, consider how you could set limits. Where could you claim more time, more space for yourself? How, and to whom, could you say “no" or "not now” with consequences you could live with?

It is too tempting to say “no” and “not now” to your own needs instead of to the people around you. The problem with that strategy is that in the long run, this is a recipe for burnout. While flexibility might be admirable, it can be an impediment to holding on to balance. Flexibility still needs to suit your own needs to be sustainable.

Einstein once said, "Life is like a bicycle. To keep your balance, you must keep moving."

Figuring out the best "moves" and continuing to do them is how you cultivate balance and resilience. Indeed, it is only when you're pulled off balance that you're reminded how to stand tall.

#4789. Taking Blood Pressure Meds? DASH Diet Likely Safe for Potassium Levels

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

People who adhere to the Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet do not experience significant changes in potassium levels while taking blood pressure medications or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory (NSAID) drugs, according to a new study.

Researchers also reported that people taking these medications do not experience significant changes in their kidney function.

Both types of medications are known to increase potassium levels. High potassium levels can lead to hyperkalemia, a condition that can cause issues with the heart rhythm. People with impaired kidney function due to chronic kidney disease are at increased risk of hyperkalemia.

“The DASH diet is a well-known, proven nutrition pattern that is known to improve blood pressure,” said Marian Budu, MD, a clinical research coordinator on the GoFresh Trials at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston and the presenting author of the study, in a news release.

“Knowing that the DASH diet did not increase blood potassium levels in this population with normal baseline potassium levels provides assurance that the DASH diet can be prescribed to a wide range of people,” she continued.

The preliminary findings are being presented at the American Heart Association’s Hypertension Scientific Sessions 2026 meeting this week in Virginia. The research has not been published yet in a peer-reviewed journal.

Experts not involved in the study told Healthline that the research provides medical professionals with important information.

“While we have traditionally exercised caution before recommending the DASH diet in patients who are prescribed ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, or potassium-sparing diuretics, these results show that those patients could likely adopt the DASH diet without significant concern for harm,” said Cheng-Han Chen, MD, an interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center in Laguna Hills, CA.

“DASH diets do not appear to increase potassium levels to any significant degree in patients taking medications that are known to potentially raise serum potassium,” added Kevin Volpp, MD, the founding director of the Penn Center for Health Incentives and Behavioral Economics in Pennsylvania and the scientific lead of the American Heart Association’s Health Care by Food initiative.

“This is important because it is a theoretical concern that diets rich in potassium could cause high levels in potassium in some patients.”

The new study was a secondary analysis of the GoFresh and GoFresh Rx randomized trials that enrolled Black adults in the greater Boston area with high blood pressure.

Some of the participants were taking medications to lower their blood pressure, and others were not taking any hypertension drugs.

The study focused on four classes of blood pressure medications: angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEi), angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), and potassium-sparing diuretics and beta-blockers, as well as NSAIDs.

The analysis took place in 2026 and included 356 Black adults with an average age of 53. About 70% were women.

At the start of the study, the participants had systolic blood pressure readings between 120 mm Hg and less than 150 mm Hg. They also had a diastolic blood pressure reading of less than 100 mm Hg.

The participants also had varying degrees of kidney function. In addition, they had limited access to grocery stores.

Half of the participants received three months of weekly DASH-patterned groceries and weekly nutrition counseling sessions. The other half received a cash stipend every four weeks to buy groceries, with no nutrition counseling.

The participants’ blood potassium levels were measured at the beginning of the study and again after 12 weeks.

The researchers reported that eating more potassium-rich foods in the DASH diet did not increase potassium levels to dangerous levels among participants taking blood pressure medications.

They noted no significant increase in potassium levels, regardless of whether participants were assigned to the dietary intervention or the monetary stipend group.

In a news release, the researchers acknowledged that their study did not include people with stage 4 or stage 5 kidney disease or those with higher-than-normal potassium levels.

They added that the study population comprised only Black individuals living in Boston, so the results may not generalize to the broader population.

The study authors said that future research should focus on participants with suboptimal kidney function and those with higher potassium levels.

Volpp agreed that more research is needed.

“This study was conducted in patients with non-elevated potassium levels at baseline and does not answer the question of whether they are safe in patients with elevated potassium levels or significant impairments in renal function,” he told Healthline.

Chen noted that potassium levels should be taken seriously.

“Certain classes of blood pressure medications can potentially cause high potassium levels, especially in people with kidney disease,” he told Healthline. “If potassium levels become too high, this can lead to symptoms such as fatigue, nausea, and muscle pain, or even serious heart problems such as arrhythmias.”

The DASH diet is a dietary plan that emphasizes fruits, vegetables, and lean proteins such as chicken, fish, and beans.

The plan also includes whole grains, low fat dairy products, and cooking with vegetable oils. The diet discourages the intake of red meat, salt, fat, and added sugars.

Previous research has indicated that the DASH diet can provide numerous health benefits.

A preliminary 2022 study concluded that the dietary plan can help lower blood pressure and improve heart health, but those results haven’t been published in a scientific journal. Still, the findings were consistent with a 2019 study that found the DASH diet can help lower the risk of heart disease.

In addition, a 2020 study reported that adults aged 65 and older with obesity lost body fat while following the DASH Diet. A 2023 study suggested the diet can help reduce belly fat.

A 2019 meta-analysis suggested that the DASH diet may also help lower the risk of certain cancers.

Many of these protective effects are attributed to the diet’s high fruit and vegetable content.

Chen said the DASH diet has many benefits, but the eating plan might not be for everybody.

“The DASH diet has been shown to be beneficial in lowering blood pressure, losing weight, and controlling blood sugar and cholesterol levels,” he said. “However, the amount of planning and portion tracking required to follow the diet may be too much for some people.”

Chen recommended that people ease into the DASH diet.

“The best way to start on the DASH diet is to slowly introduce the changes to your meals,” he said. “This can be as simple as including a few extra servings of fruits and vegetables each day as well as swapping some whole grain products for refined grains. Over time, more of the diet can be incorporated.”

Volpp agreed that introducing the DASH diet in increments is a good strategy.

“For many people, it is easiest to make small incremental changes sequentially,” he said. “One way to get started is to increase fruit by a couple of servings a day. Another is to pay attention to the amount of sodium in packaged foods and consciously choose products lower in sodium. A third is to make a conscious effort to eat more vegetables.”

“Make changes first that are easiest for you to make; it will be easier to make those changes stick,” Volpp added.
